newsitem.title: USA: US banks cut provisions against bad loans -- SF Fed.
newsitem.headline: US banks cut provisions against bad loans -- SF Fed.

text.p: As the U.S. economy gallops into its seventh year of expansion and abundant credit, banks have been setting aside less money for provisions against possible bad loans, said an official at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco.
"This has some to do with the good credit experience in most of the commercial banks," Simon Kwan, an economist at the San Francisco Fed research department, told Reuters.
"We are at a very good part of the credit cycle in terms of deliquency and default rates ... Both consumer loans and consumer loan deliquency have levelled off," Kwan added.
The Fed economist said, however, this situation could not be prolonged indefinitely.
Although he declined to make predictions on when banks would have to start increasing their loan loss provisions, he said he believed the credit cycle was getting ripe.
"We're almost at the peak of the credit cycle and we do not know how long will the good times will last, (but) the loan loss reserve ratio simply cannot keep falling indefinitely," Kwan said.
"At some point in time (banks) have to ... start to build up their reserves against future losses," he added.

The U.S. banks' loan loss reserve ratio -- the amount of cash set aside by banks as a percentage of total outstanding loans -- is currently ranging between 1.7 and 2.0 percent, depending on the institution.
Those figures are still high compared to historical lows of 1.0 percent in the late 1970s.

But they are well below the record highs of 2.5 percent seen in the late 1980s, when banks raised provisions dramatically on fears that less developed countries, particularly in Latin America, would default on their long-term loans.
For now, analysts said the Fed appears to be content with the current amount of credit available in the economy.

An indication of that, the pundits said, was the fact that the central bank decided to keep monetary policy unchanged at the last two meetings of its policy-setting body after having raised the federal funds rate in March.
The fed funds rate is currently targeted at 5.50 percent by the central bank.
President of the Minneapolis Fed, Gary Stern, said late last week he saw no credit constraints in the economy, with the exception, perhaps, of some tighteness in the consumer sector.

"We don't perceive there is a shortage of credit in agricultural or any other sector of the economy. Credit is readily available, but one place where it might be a touch tighter is on the consumer side," Stern said.

Banks have nothing to complain about with the current situation. The San Francisco Fed economist said the declining loan loss provision has contributed to a sharp increase in financial institutions' profits in recent years.
"Banks have been making record profits in terms of earnings, equities and assets," Kwan said.
"(But) we have noticed that one of the factors contributing to strong earnings is the fact that (banks) have been providing smaller-than-usual loan loss provisions," the Fed economist added.
Loan loss provisions are charged against operating earnings, Kwan said.
